newsitem.title: CROATIA: Machinegun attack wounds moderate Croat politician.
newsitem.headline: Machinegun attack wounds moderate Croat politician.

text.p: A Bosnian Croat opposition leader and his wife were wounded in a machinegun attack on their home in Mostar, the European Union mission in the gangster-ridden city said on Tuesday.

An EU statement said unidentified assailants opened fire from a car on Monday night on the home of moderate coalition leader Jole Musa in the west half of Mostar, which is ruled by Croat ultra-nationalists.
"Both Mr Musa and his wife were injured in the attack. Mr Musa required hospital treatment," the statement said.

HINA, the Croatian state news agency, said Musa, who is in late middle age, was expected to undergo surgery for a wound in the groin. His condition was not life-threatening, it quoted doctors as saying.
Croat police in west Mostar said the assailants targeted the living room of the home where Musa and his wife, Vera, were sitting at the time.
Western European Union and local police had begun a joint investigation.
It was not the first incident at Musa's home. An explosive like a large firecracker was thrown at the house on Saturday, shattering a window. There were no injuries.

Special EU envoy Sir Martin Garrod deplored the attack on Musa. He heads a two-year-old mission working to reunite sectors of Mostar held by Moslem and Croat nationalists, who ripped the city apart in war.
"Sir Martin expresses serious concern about the possible consequences of this attack on the process of normalisation in Mostar," the EU statement said.
"He urges leaders at all levels to do their utmost to ensure that those responsible are brought to justice as soon as possible."

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe also strongly comdemned the attack and called on the competent authorities to "urgently investigate the case and bring the perpetrators to justice."
The Croatian mayor of the western Bosnian town of Mostar, Ivan Prskalo, described the shooting on Monday as a "grave incident".
He said the future had to be built on respect for basic human rights and the freedoms of all citizens of Mostar.

"I believe that the irresponsible perpetrators...are not aware of how such actions threaten in a most direct way the unity of all Croats which we need so much," Croatian radio quoted Prskalo as saying.

Analysts said the perpetrators were probably right-wing paramilitary gangsters who pervade the Croat power structure in Mostar and are hostile to Musa's platform of reconciliation and power-sharing with Moslems.
Musa won a parliamentary seat in Bosnia's September 14 general elections that were prescribed by the 1995 Dayton peace treaty to help reunify a country torn apart in 43 months of nationalist war.
A joint city council was formed in Mostar in August after Croat nationalists ended a boycott imposed after municipal polls in the city, but the new governing body is toothless.
